title: Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows and Risk Exceptions
author: Jordan Patel
content:
Summary:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s security and compliance controls covering Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging and retention, data residency and retention requirements, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) controls, security-focused incident response procedures, compliance evidence collection and workflows, and the process for managing risk and exceptions. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders who implement and operate Redwood’s platform across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood production and staging environments, customer-managed Private deployments, and administrative consoles.
- Covers platform services (control plane), serving runtime components, observability tooling (logging/metrics/tracing), and build/pipeline artifacts used to produce deployables.

Goals:
- Ensure least-privilege access across systems through consistent RBAC policies.
- Provide tamper-evident audit trails with defined retention and replayability for investigations and compliance audits.
- Maintain clear data residency and retention policies aligned to customer contracts and regulatory obligations.
- Integrate security gates into the SDLC to prevent regressions.
- Define operational incident procedures with roles and evidence-preservation steps.
- Provide a repeatable compliance evidence collection workflow for audits.

Roles and Responsibilities:
- Security (owner): overall policy authorship, exception approvals, quarterly control reviews.
- Eng Infra (owner): implement and maintain IAM, network guardrails, key management integrations.
- Eng SRE (owner): logging ingestion, retention enforcement, alerting on suspicious activity.
- Product/Legal: define customer residency/retention contract terms and compliance scope.
- Engineering teams: implement least-privilege roles in services they own, ensure pipelines follow SDLC gates.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview:
Redwood uses a centralized identity and access management model backed by single sign-on (SSO) and group-based roles for human users and scoped service principals for non-human access. The goal is least-privilege access with time-bound elevated access where needed.

Key controls:
- Identity provider: Okta (primary) for Redwood hosted control plane and Google Workspace for legacy integration.
- Authentication: SSO with enforced MFA (TOTP + hardware token for privileged roles).
- Service principals: short-lived certificates or OAuth2 client credentials rotated every 30 days by default.
- Role model: map of canonical roles (Owner, Admin, Operator, Developer, ReadOnly) applied consistently across services.
- Approval workflow: all Admin/Owner role assignments require a 2-approver approval flow recorded in the access request system (Concourse Access Requests).
- Access reviews: quarterly automated access reviews with manual remediation required within 7 days for stale memberships.

RBAC matrix (examples):
| Role | Platform Console | Cluster/Admin API | Logging/Tracing | Billing | Secrets/KMS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Owner | full | full | full | full | view+approve |
| Admin | manage-users | manage | manage | view | decrypt |
| Operator | deploy/restart | manage-routes | view | none | none |
| Developer | deploy | limited | view | none | none |
| ReadOnly | view | view | view | view | none |

Access-request procedure (high-level):
1. Engineer requests role via Access Requests app with justification and duration (max 90 days for temporary admin).
2. Two approvers (team manager + security owner) approve or reject.
3. Requests are logged to audit log channel and ticket created in Jira for record.

Service-to-service auth:
- Mutual TLS within VPCs/regions for internal traffic.
- JWTs signed by internal CA for cross-service calls with audience and scope claims.
- Token lifetime: default 15 minutes; refresh tokens limited to service principals with rotation.

2) Audit Logging

Objectives:
- Provide tamper-evident logs for authentication events, privileged operations, configuration changes, and sensitive data access.
- Support forensic investigations and compliance evidence requests.

What we capture:
- Authentication events: successful/failed logins, MFA events, password changes.
- Authorization events: role assignments, policy changes, temporary elevation grants.
- Admin actions: user creation/deletion, model deployment rollouts, canary switchovers, infrastructure changes (IAM, network).
- Data access events: decryption operations, KMS usage, customer data exports.
- System events: service restarts, configuration changes, scaling actions.

Logging pipeline and retention:
- Ingestion: Fluentd -> central logging cluster (Elasticsearch-compatible) with Kafka buffering for durability.
- Integrity: logs are hashed and periodically anchored to an external immutable store (S3 with object lock and AWS KMS) to provide tamper evidence.
- Retention policy (default):
  - Critical security logs (authN/authZ, admin actions): 2 years (archive after 365 days to WORM storage).
  - High-value operational logs (deployments, rollouts): 1 year.
  - Application level debug logs: 90 days.
  - PII access audit events: retained for 3 years or per contract if longer.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Suspicious auth patterns (multiple failed logins + sign-in from new geo): P1 alert to SecOps.
- Privilege escalation events: P1 alert.
- Bulk data export: P1 with automatic session freeze for the initiating account pending investigation.

Audit access controls:
- Access to raw logs requires Audit_Read role and an approval ticket for extraction.
- Extraction of logs for external auditors is performed by Security with redaction as needed.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles:
- Customer data is stored only in regions agreed in the contract.
- Control plane metadata and telemetry are subject to internal residency policy and may be aggregated across regions, but customer PII is scoped to the customer’s region.

Supported regions and residency mapping:
- US: us-east-1 (primary), us-west-2 (secondary failover)
- EU: eu-west-1
- APAC: ap-southeast-1 (select enterprise customers)

Key controls:
- Region tagging: all storage resources must include region and data-class tags.
- Network controls: VPC endpoints and restricted egress for Private deployments to prevent cross-region replication unless explicitly configured.
- Encryption: at-rest encryption with AWS KMS customer-managed keys (CMKs) for enterprise customers; HSM integration for on-prem private deployments.

Retention schedules (baseline):
| Data class | Production retention | Archive retention | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Authentication & Authorization logs | 2 years | 7 years (upon legal hold) | Critical for investigations |
| Customer customer-data (non-PII) | 1 year | 3 years | Per contract overrides |
| Customer PII | per-contract (default 7 years) | archived to WORM on request | Data subject to local laws (e.g., GDPR erasure) |
| Backups & snapshots | 90 days | 365 days (archived) | Encrypted with CMK |

Data deletion and egress requests:
- Data subject access and deletion requests are handled by Product & Legal with Engineering support.
- Deletion includes: database deletion, object store purge, and cryptographic key rotation where relevant.
- Egress/export requests must be logged; exports of PII require a Data Export Approval ticket and security review.

4) Secure SDLC (Security Controls in Build & Deploy)

Gate definitions:
- Code review: all PRs require 1 peer review and one security automated check pass.
- Static analysis: SAST run on every PR (critical blockers must be fixed before merge).
- Dependency scanning: SBOM generated for every release and automated dependency vulnerability scanning (block on CVSS >= 9.0 for direct dependencies).
- Secrets scanning: pre-commit hooks + CI secret scanning; any secret found triggers immediate rotation and incident process.
- Infrastructure as Code (IaC) scanning: policies enforced in CI (Terraform validate + tfsec/policy-as-code).
- Runtime security tests: dynamic scanning in staging and canary environments, including fuzzing and adversarial prompt tests for model-serving endpoints.

Release checklist (for services handling customer data):
1. PRs merged with passing CI and SAST/SCA results.
2. SBOM & vulnerability report attached to release.
3. Pentests/third-party scans completed for major changes (annually for core services).
4. Feature flags for rollout and immediate rollback plan documented.
5. Observability hooks (tracing, metrics, audit events) present for all new code paths.
6. Deployment to canary region with automated smoke tests for 48 hours before global rollout.

Developer privileges during CI/CD:
- CI service uses ephemeral credentials scoped to the pipeline.
- Approvals for production deploys require Operator role sign-off and automated gating by security tests.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Objectives:
- Contain and eradicate active security incidents quickly while preserving evidence.
- Communicate with stakeholders and customers per incident classification.

Incident classification:
- P0 (data exfiltration / confirmed breach)
- P1 (privilege escalation, large-scale account compromise)
- P2 (service degradation with potential security impact)

Initial triage checklist (first 60 minutes):
1. Triage lead assigned (on-call SecOps).
2. Capture live evidence: snapshots of affected hosts, memory if feasible, and relevant log ranges (note retention pointers).
3. Isolate impacted systems (network quiesce or flow control) to stop spread.
4. Rotate credentials and invalidate tokens for impacted principals.
5. Notify Legal and Execs for P0/P1 incidents.

Forensics & evidence preservation:
- Use immutable log indexes and S3 object lock snapshots.
- Create an evidence bundle with chain-of-custody metadata (collected by SecOps): list of files, hashes, collection time, collector.
- Preserve copies in a dedicated secure evidence bucket with restricted access and 7-year retention for P0 incidents.

Customer notification timeline:
- P0: initial notification within 72 hours (as required by law and contract), followed by status updates every 24 hours until resolved.
- P1/P2: notification per contractual SLAs and legal guidance.

Post-incident actions:
- Root cause analysis and remediation plan within 7 calendar days.
- Postmortem published in oncall-and-incident-response with redacted customer data and lessons learned.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose:
Provide a documented, repeatable process to collect, redact, and deliver evidence for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, customer audits).

Evidence types and owners:
- Policy documents (Security) — Security owner
- Access logs and audit trails (SRE/SecOps) — SRE owner collects and validates hashes
- Configuration snapshots (Infra) — Eng Infra owner
- Code & pipeline artifacts (Eng DX/CI) — Eng Developer Experience owner
- Pen test reports & vulnerability scans (Security) — Security owner

Workflow (high-level):
1. Audit request intake (Compliance team logs request with scope and timeframe).
2. Security triages scope and identifies required artifacts.
3. Owners generate evidence exports into a secure staging bucket.
4. Evidence redaction: Security reviews artifacts for PII and sensitive operational details; redaction performed where required.
5. Evidence delivery: provide auditors with time-bound access or bundle exports with README and hashes.
6. Record retention: evidence packages are recorded in the Audit Evidence Registry with retention per audit contract (default 7 years).

Automation & tooling:
- Use the Audit Evidence Bot to collate and hash artifacts, generate README, and create tickets for manual redaction steps.
- Tamper-evidence: all bundles include a signed manifest with SHA256 checksums and signer identity.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

When controls cannot be met due to technical or business constraints, teams must request a formal exception. Exceptions are time-bound and require compensating controls.

Exception request procedure:
1. Submit exception via the Exceptions Registry with: rationale, impacted control(s), proposed compensating controls, risk assessment, owner, and desired TTL (max 90 days for initial approval).
2. Security reviews within 5 business days and assigns a risk owner.
3. If high-risk, presentation to Risk Committee required.
4. Approved exceptions issued with mandatory mitigation tasks and monitoring requirements.

Compensating controls examples:
- If full IAM integration is delayed for a Private deployment: require network isolation and daily attestations of access lists, with weekly audit extracts sent to Security.
- If audit log forwarding cannot be implemented immediately: provision local immutable collection and perform manual daily sync to central store until automated pipeline is available.

Expiration and renewal:
- Exceptions auto-expire at TTL; owners must submit renewal with evidence of progress.
- Unrenewed exceptions are escalated and remediated by Infra/Security.

8) Metrics and Reporting

Key metrics to track (report monthly to Security & Exec):
- Number of privileged (Admin/Owner) accounts and change from prior period.
- Number of access requests & average approval time.
- Number of audit log gaps and ingestion failures.
- Time to contain for P0/P1 incidents.
- Open exceptions and average age.

Quarterly reviews:
- Security runs a quarterly control effectiveness review and publishes a control health dashboard in the Security space.
